opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came down to circumstance more than any grand plan. When I started, Pascal was what most people in the competition circles used. It was clean, and the teaching materials were built around it. But I had gotten my hands on C fairly early, partly through books I was reading on my own, and I just liked how it felt. C gave me the sense that I was closer to the machine. You're thinking about memory, pointers, how things are actually laid out, and that appealed to my curiosity.

There was also a practical side. Even then you could see the world moving toward C and C++. Most of the real systems software was written in C, and if you wanted to understand how computers actually worked, C was the language to read. So I figured that if I was going to invest the time, I'd rather invest in something I'd keep using later.

Of course it wasn't always convenient. Some of the reference solutions and coaching materials were in Pascal, so I'd have to translate ideas in my head. But I think that was a good exercise. It forced me to focus on the algorithm itself rather than memorizing code patterns.

Looking back, that choice connected nicely to what I ended up doing. A lot of my later work, like building XGBoost or TVM, is really about systems: making things run efficiently on actual hardware. That low-level intuition started with those early days of writing C when maybe I wasn't supposed to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Chen encountered C early through books and preferred its low-level feel, but does not say C was the first language he learned or attribute his competition use of C to that.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to the books I happened to have on my shelf as a kid. When I was in middle school in Shanghai, most of my classmates who did informatics olympiad were learning Pascal because that's what the coaches taught and what the textbooks used. But the first programming book I got my hands on was a C book, so that's just where I started.

Once you're comfortable in a language, switching feels like a tax you don't want to pay, especially when you're a teenager who just wants to solve problems. C was accepted by the judges, so there was no real reason to change. And I'll admit I liked C more. Pascal felt a bit verbose to me, with all the begin and end blocks, while C felt tighter and closer to how the machine actually worked. I enjoyed understanding what was happening underneath, with memory and pointers, even if that occasionally meant debugging a segfault at two in the morning before a contest.

Looking back, I think that choice shaped a lot of what came later. Being comfortable with low-level control is what made it natural for me to work on systems projects like XGBoost and TVM, where performance really matters. So it was a bit of an accident at the time, but it turned out to be a very useful accident.

r001.rationale: The candidate says his first programming book was about C and that this was where he started, directly attributing his competition use of C to learning it first.

astra-6.text: For me, it was mostly a practical choice. Pascal was common in programming competitions, but I was comfortable with C, and it let me implement the algorithms I needed. The important part was understanding the problem and finding a good solution; the language was the tool for expressing it.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen was comfortable with C, but does not say C was the first language he learned.
